speechtext:
I wish to reply to another question relating to international affairs asked yesterday by the hon. member for St. Law-rence-St. George (Mr. Cahan), in respect to the ratification of the Canada-France convention. Following approval by the Canadian parliament, the convention concerning the rights of nationals and commercial and shipping matters between Canada and France was ratified by the king in respect of Canada on June 30, 1933. No steps have yet been taken to arrange for the exchange of ratifications under article 21 of the convention, as ratification has not yet been effected by the appropriate authorities of the French republic. A Senate committee last week made a report favouring ratification of this convention.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I am sorry I did not hear the hon. gentleman.

I was a member of the
last parliament, Mr. Chairman, and we had a committee on housing and reconstruction which went into the class of materials dealt with in item 503, in connection with housing and reconstruction. What the hon. member for Dauphin (Mr. Ward) said last night was illuminating as far as it went, but he left out the main facts, and after all facts are facts. What happened to the lumber industry in this country under the free trade policy of the Liberal government? Some hon. gentlemen talk about taking the tariff out of politics, but it never will be taken out of politics and it is a blessing that it never can be, because tihe tariff vitally concerns the jobs and livelihood of the vast majority of our population.
As I was saying, we had a committee of this house appointed last year to look into housing and reconstruction, and I want to say a few words in reply to my hon. friend from Dauphin, who talks about the vast number of men who were thrown out of employment in this country in consequence of the action of the United States government imposing a duty of four dollars per thousand feet on the importation of Canadian lumber, as compared with the duty of one dollar per thousand feet which previously prevailed. Why, Mr. Chairman, in the United States they had nearly twenty-four million people unemployed, fourteen million living on relief works, and ten million on direct relief, and they had to introduce the NRA and go into large reconstruction and housing schemes to give em-

Canada-U. S. Trade Agreement
ployment to their idle workingmen. Materials, planks, boards and everything else required in housing had to be supplied.
I have before me the report of the assessment commissioner for Toronto showing how the construction industry has contracted in recent years. Conditions on this continent are very different from conditions in Italy, where lumber is being used to build municipal institutions to satisfy the requirements of the next twenty-five, years, for court houses, all kinds of hospitals, and many other public buildings, and Italy, of course, is providing the labour and the materials.
The investigation that was made by the parliamentary committee places the matter in an entirely different light from that presented last night by the hon. member for Dauphin.
Here we are in this particular committee, composed of 245 members of the House of Commons, considering the different items in this trade agreement. Can you imagine any business trying to conduct its affairs in a committee of 245 members? We have been discussing this trade agreement for five or six days, and it is said that we must not yet look at schedule II. As a matter of fact the United States is giving us nothing but gold bricks, while we are giving them extremely valuable concessions. And you, Mr. Chairman, preside over this committee of 245 members. You are really the chief coroner, because we are just holding a post mortem; everything in this agreement is already signed, sealed and delivered. Our hands are tied and we can do nothing about it; we cannot change a word of it. There is no reciprocity at all in this agreement. The President of the United States himself in his message to congress said that his powers in making tariff changes were limited by the constitution to a change of not more than fifty per cent in the tariff in connection with any foreign trade agreement. We are giving the United States the benefit of our intermediate tariff. We are admitting many of their products free, and in return we get very little. Business people here in Canada to-day have to pay duplicate, and in some cases triplicate, income taxes. It means that any benefit that might have been coming to men in the building industry will be more than wiped out by the taxes they will have to pay. Many of these men are being driven to the wall. But here we are, sitting in a committee of 245, considering item 503, and we cannot change one word of it or of any other item in this agreement. We have to take the whole thing as it stands because any amendment vitiates the whole agreement. As the Prime Minister has said,
l*Mr. Church.]
we cannot change it to the extent of dotting an "i" or crossing a "t". I should like to have moved that this item be struck out altogether, Mr. Chairman, but parliamentary rules prevent me from doing that. One of the main things we need in this country is constitutional reform, so that we can properly consider these important matters. We have been sitting here five or six days talking about an agreement that has been signed, sealed and delivered, and the free representatives of the people in this parliament might just as well not be here for all they can do about it.
Ministers and ambassadors from this country have gone down to Washington in years gone by and have come back with far better agreements than this. I see my hon. friend from North Huron (Mr. Deachman) in his seat. He had something to say about this agreement yesterday. At one time he was a supporter of the government of Mr. Drury in the province of Ontario. In 1924, on April 2, representatives of the Canadian Council of Agriculture came to Ottawa and presented to the cabinet a memorandum in which they urged that relief be granted to the agricultural industry. Mr. Drury denounced the manufacturers as thieves and robbers and asked for free trade, not only in agricultural products but in lumber. They threw away a whole principality of timber to an American millionaire, Mr. Backus. Such happenings run through the whole history of the lumbering industry of this country, and of Ontario in particular.
Will the hon. gentleman kindly keep to the item under discussion? I do not think that Mr. Drury has anything to do with this item.

I do not think it is
necessary for you to speak in that way, Mr. Chairman; I know the rules as well as you do. They have been read three or four times already. As I say, this is only a post mortem examination. They have tried to make a lethal chamber out of this place and the Minister of Finance has been appointed the lord high executioner. He is a very capable executioner. If you do not want any more discussion on this item, I can only say that for twelve years Mr. Drury tried to have this free trade lumber provision put into effect. If I am not entitled to discuss the principle involved in this item, you can rule me out of order. I do not wish to say anything further if we cannot discuss the principle of this item. The hon. member for Dauphin (Mr. Ward) was allowed to discuss agricultural implements last night; he wandered all over the different tariffs put

Canada-U. S. Trade Agreement
into effect by the last three or four presidents of the United States, but when a member of the opposition gets up to discuss the principle of this item he is told he is out of order. The principle in this vole is the relief of unemployment, and it is relevant.
What is the minister doing with the experts in the tariff board? As I read the statutes, no change can be made in the tariff of this country unless approved by that body. I contend that this agreement is out of order for that reason, and that it would be declared ultra vires if sent to the courts. There are many experts on this agreement under the lord high executioner; he has in front of him two of the finest young men we have in the civil service. We are fortunate to have such gentlemen in the service and I ask him if they recommended this change.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: There is no change. This item has been free and it will remain free.

What is this big tariff
board of this and other governments doing? They might just as well be a travelling minstrel show with their faces blacked. All they do is act as doctors, chopping off a limb there and a limb here. This item was not free before this agreement. The United States tariff was one dollar per thousand, and then four dollars.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Your government
appointed them.

Away back in 1911 this
very same item was considered by Mr. Paterson and Mr. Fielding. This was considered back in the days of Sir Wilfrid Laurier and the present government does not realize that this proposition will make a Lazarus out of a country that Sir Wilfrid Laurier professed to have made a nation. We are going to have so much free trade that no man will put a dollar into industry. Mr. Drury made new Ontario the happy hunting ground for the American millionaire. They crossed into this country and bought up all the timber limits. Only the other day a carload of lumber came into Ottawa under this item. Where is that lumber? It is down in the Rideau canal beside the Chateau Laurier being used to fix u,p Canada's new navy of tugs, and scows, and other such craft. The people of this country should not have to pay more for any commodity because of any combine which might exist. I suggest that the Minister of Finance and his experts should decide a fair amount to be allowed for labour and profit-in the manufacture of agricultural implements and other articles. The remainder could be considered an excise tax to be paid into the federal treasury. That would be
real protection, not only for the agricultural implement industry but for the consumers as well.
There are many industries in my riding, and during the time I spent in public office many millions of dollars' worth of lumber were purchased. Practically all the lumber used by the Toronto harbour commission was brought in from British Columbia through the Panama Canal. This was done in order to help the lumbering industry in British Columbia. The Minister of Labour (Mr. Rogers) is not in the chamber, but I think he should make a statement with reference to these items. Only one man knows anything about this American agreement and he negotiated it so quickly that he ignored entirely the high court of parliament. Talk about Hitler and Mussolini; this is just as bad as anything they ever did. They could not get away with similar action down in Washington. Our Senate has gone on a holiday instead of holding an investigation to help this committee. Is the committee aware that an investigation is now being conducted by the senate in Washington into what is known as the lobby inquiry presided over by Senator Black. This committee is investigating the lobbying which has been carried on at Washington by industry, the tactics referred to last night by the senior member of my party. It has been shown that
7,000	false telegrams were sent out in an effort to influence the newspapers and various important people throughout the country about tariff legislation. The New York Times of March 3 contains an article giving a full account of what has been going on before this committee, and the Ottawa Journal of this morning makes reference to the same investigation.
The whole agreement should be referred to the tariff board. What is the use of having a tariff board? It is ridiculous and a squandering of the taxpayers' money to have a tariff board with its many experts not doing the work it should be doing. Business men in Ontario are wondering how long this free trade is going to continue. I know of one factory which intended to put on more men, but when the manager saw this article about the tariff he decided not to increase his staff. We should have some explanation from the government of the day as to why these duties have been removed. A royal commission has been appointed to study the textile industry; one should be appointed to study the lumbering industry before we approve this agreement. Timber limits all over the country have been given away to Americans by Liberal governments. I can remember when Peter Ryan was appointed an auctioneer to auction off these

Canada-U. S. Trade Agreement
limits and nearly three-quarters of the bidders for timber berths were Americans. They came over here and they found Canada a happy hunting ground.
The more I study this agreement the more I believe the people should vote on it. We cannot vote on it. As the Prime Minister has said, this is a treaty which has been signed, sealed and delivered. It has been agreed to by the two high contracting parties, Canada and the United States, and we cannot do anything about it. We can go on talking about it, but nothing plus nothing equals nothing; we might just as well go back home and tell our constituents that there is no such thing as constitutional government in this country.

Mr. Chairman, I represent
the riding of Colchester-Hants where the people are very much interested in the lumbering business. Being engaged in that business myself I should like to say a word before this item carries. I was rather amused to hear what hon. members on the opposition benches had to say with respect to our trade with the United States. They refused to accept responsibility for the great drop in our trade with the republic to the south; they said they had nothing to do with it and that it was not a measure of retaliation on the part of the United States which prevented our Canadian lumber from going in. Surely they will grant that when they came into power in 1930 we had a market of $56,000,000 in the United States whereas when they went out of power that market, for lumber and lumber products, had been reduced to $10,000,000. Now they turn around and claim to have saved the lumber industry of Canada by means of the empire trade agreements. But what did those agreements do for our lumber? What they did was to bind the duty already existing on certain classes of material. What has really happened is this, that to-day the price in sterling we are getting in the old country for our lumber is not as favourable as the price we received before the empire agreements came into force. The value of the pound sterling has risen from around $4.25 to about $5. I do not think that our friends in the opposition can take credit for that, and therefore they are not entitled to take credit for any great increase in the export of lumber to the United Kingdom.
My hon. friend from Royal (Mr. Brooks) the other night said that the trade agreement would do the maritimes no good; he said that the people there were still selling lumber to the United Kingdom and could not sell to the United States. If he had inquired further he would have found the reason why the mari-

time lumbermen are to-day able to secure a better market in the old country for their products. The answer was given yesterday by the hon. member for Dauphin (Mr. Ward) when he pointed out that the British Columbia lumbermen are now sending their lumber into the United States, and this having released the pressure on the English market has allowed the maritime lumbermen to sell their products there. So far as the maritime lumbermen are concerned, we are shipping into the United States a good deal more lumber than we did before the treaty was signed. If you will look around in Nova Scotia and New Brunswick you will see a great many lumbermen preparing to ship in the summer when navigation opens up, and therefore as regards the maritimes the treaty will be of considerable benefit.

I had hoped last night
that we should be able to finish the whole of this schedule. About a quarter to eleven the item was really passed and then there took place some discussion which seems to have obscured the situation. I suggest that we wandered rather far away from the particular item under consideration and I would also suggest that we pass the item, and if we have further questions to ask we might take them up in connection with schedule II with regard to lumber.

speechtext: I think that is true.

The duty has not been reduced very much unless the 4 cents a pound is taken into consideration. On looking up the trade figures I note that the poundage is mentioned in connection with each figure. In 1931 we imported from the United States 8279,000 whereas in 1935 but as a result to a percentage of the late government's protective policy, we imported only $20,000 worth. It appears that we have been importing this line more extensively from Great Britain than from the United States, for in 1931 we imported 8371,000 and in 1935, 8165,000. These figures are taken from page 514 of the large trade return book. In reference to that book, I should like to say in passing that when the minister inquired regarding the page, when I was quoting with reference to printing machinery yesterday, item 412a, b, c, and d, I referred him to pages 338 and 339. I should have said 611 and 612.
Coming back to the item under discussion, I should imagine that one result of this duty would be that importations from the United States would largely increase, and on the other hand importations from Great Britain would decline. If we have to import from outside I should be sorry to see us import more of this line of material from our cousins to the south than from our brothers in the old land. I do not know the number of men employed in this country; I could not find
out in any of the year books. But if it affects employment in Canada it will be unfortunate.

Under the
British empire agreements Canada bought about 81 worth of goods from Great Britain where they bought about S3 worth from us. Hon. gentlemen opposite seem to be very much perturbed now because the Americans might sell some of their goods in this market and affect the Britisher selling here, but they put into effect a treaty which has made it possible for the Britisher to sell only $1 worth here where we sell S3 worth over there. The main object of their agreement was to try to keep the Britisher and everybody else out of this market. I think it is about time they stopped talking about giving somebody else the opportunity that they gave Great Britain.

Did the minister give
the imports from Great Britain?

I think I shall have to
refer that question to the Minister of National Revenue. I cannot explain it.

I admit, from
the figures furnished by the minister, that

the imports were not very considerable during the last fiscal year. Of course we had an awful depression. But if times become normal our brass bands, which even now are increasing all over the country, may grow to a point where we shall have to import a large number of musical instruments, either brass finished or silver plate finished. May I suggest, if I am in order, that the duty of twenty-five per cent provided for by this agreement be reduced?
Hear, hear.

I have not finished. I am saying these things because we have no brass manufacturing industries producing musical instruments in Canada. I suggest that the tariff be reduced to 20 per cent on the purely brass and increased on the silver plated ones from 35 to 40 per cent, to give a chance to our numerous silverplating and electro-plating plants to get some work.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Oh, that is the catch
in it.

I agree with my hon. friend that we ought to reduce the tariff on the brass instruments, and I should be in favour of reducing the duty on silver ones too. Throughout Canada at the present time we have many returned soldier bands the members of which are spending a good deal of their own money in order to maintain them, and the instruments cost them a considerable amount. I think that we should make an exception in such cases; if they want to import instruments for the purposes of the bands they should be allowed to bring them in free.
You are magnanimous.

I admit the force of what the hon. member for Moose Jaw (Mr. Ross) has said. But you must also bear in mind the fact that most of the brass bands of this country, especially in the two oldest provinces, are made up of boys. They are subsidized either by civic authorities or, as in the province of Quebec, by religious authorities. The cost is considerable. If you reduce the duty on the brass finished products, after a while those who at the beginning of their musical career are enabled in this way to purchase a purely brass instrument may, if they find they have the talent and the natural disposition to continue, acquire a gold plated or silver plated instrument. By this means we shall be enabled to give work to numerous concerns-and I have here a list of about

twenty-five silver plating industries in Montreal-which are practically idle now; they have no trade.

speechtext: That is the next item.

It refers to this one, 599. The people of the city of Toronto take a great deal of interest in the maritime provinces, and when a member writes me it is my duty to express not only his view but my own. This particular industry used to employ a great deal of labour in the largest cities of Canada. The fur trade is an old industry, since the days that The Company of One Hundred Associates sailed up the St. Lawrence. There was some protection for them then; there is none for them now.
We have heard a good deal about how this relates to unemployment. I say it is going to have a very serious effect, not only in

the maritime provinces which supply the needs of that district but also in the central provinces of Canada where the large markets are located. In a recent issue of the Cleveland News I find this paragraph:
Figures from the League of Nations and from Washington about the decrease in unemployment since March, 1933, show that we are lagging behind Canada, Sweden, Belgium and Great Britain, and that we are just a trifle ahead of Japan. If you remove these tariff barriers you are going to create more unemployment. I should like to quote from a letter I have received in connection with this fur item from Mr. Mc-Lure, former member for Queens, Prince Edward Island:
Re Canadian tariff items 599-601; Article 3, Schedule 1. Also United States Tariff Act 1930, item 1681, of Article 4, Schedule 2. In this tariff item you will see the words "not specially provided for."
These three items are very important to the fur farmers of Canada, and especially so to the silver fox farmers of Prince Edward Island', who are the pioneers of fur farming conservation of the world.
Raw furs, or raw skins, have always been on the free list in every country in the world since Adam was a boy.
Raw furs in the early days was the currency in many countries. The United States is the only government in the world to place a duty on raw furs, with perhaps the one exception of a war tax during the Great war, when two or three countries for a short time placed a small tax on ray furs.
Briefly, the tariff is as follows: The present American duty on fox skins was imposed on June 17, 1930, and effective June 18. 1930. The provisions of the previous tariff with respect to fox skins were however unchanged.
The effective date of the last three tariff acts enacted by the Congress of the United States were as follows:	October 4,	1913;
September 22, 1922, and June 18, 1930. The sections covering fox skins under these tariffs were as follows:
1913. Paragraph 348. Furs dressed on the skin, not advanced' further than dyeing, 30 per cent ad valorem. Also paragraph 604. Skins of all kinds, raw, and hides, not specially provided for in this section.
1922. Paragraph 1420. Silver or black fox skins, dressed or undressed, not specially provided for, 50 per cent ad valorem.
1930. Paragraph 1519. Silver or black fox furs, or skins, dressed or undressed, not specially provided for, 50 per cent ad valorem.
Thus you will see that silver fox furs are the only raw furs subject to the prohibitive tariff of 50 per cent ad valorem.
The raw fur merchants of the United States are favourable to this item being on the free list; and I am certain had the Bennett government secured a treaty, that raw silver fox furs would have had consideration at least by a reduction of 50 per cent, to be 25 per cent ad valorem. The Wisconsin and Minnesota fur farmers and the farmers' bloc of the western states simply held their representatives up and secured this protection for and in the interests of their own producers.
Prince Edward Island pioneered in silver fox conservation farming and sold' breeding stock to all other countries now carrying on this industry in the different fur zones.
The United States farmers, after getting their foundation breeding stock from Canada, placed a 15 per cent duty on pure bred registered and pedigreed live silver foxes for breeding purposes (contrary I believe to all regulations regarding the interchange of pure bred stock). At the same time they placed a 50 per cent ad valorem duty on raw silver fox furs. This was in the year 1922.
Canada admits United States raw silver fox furs, and the same with all other raw furs, duty free. Now when the United States has a surplus of the low and inferior grades of raw skins they ship them into Canadian and British markets to compete and lower our prices in general.	.
We produce a better fur in Canada than in United States, generally speaking, and if we could get into the United States markets with our goods skins, even at a reduced duty of 25 per cent ad valorem, it would mean a very material advantage for our high class fox furs or raw skins. The United States is a good market, and just to show you that they cannot supply their own trade, quite a number of skins of the better grades are shipped from Canada even in the face of a 50 per cent ad valorem duty.
These tariff items that I have mentioned here. I believe, and I am confident that you can deal very effectively with them, and the thousands of fur farmers in every province in Canada will rise up and call you blessed. Likewise, all the raw' fur merchants in Canada and the United States.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I for one cannot hear a word my hon. friend is reading, but it is all going on Hansard. At least we should have an opportunity of hearing it. What little I do hear certainly has no bearing on the item before the committee; apparently it relates to the next item. Personally I am anxious that my hon. friend should have the greatest possible latitude, but surely there are limits.
I may tell the minister that as far as the chair is concerned item 599 was carried and item 601 was called.

I do not agree with placing this item on the free list. I just said this

Canada-U. S. Trade Agreement
gentleman had written me and I was giving his views. They are not necessarily my views, but I believe in protecting those in the fur trade, and I think this change to the free list will lead to greater unemployment. The letter from which I quoted referred to both items 599 and 601, fur skins of all kinds.

I wish to say a few words with regard to this item. I may say that my constituents are greatly interested in fox furs and in the production of furs generally, and I quite agree with what has been said by my hon. friend from Broadview. The maritime provinces are probably the home of the fox fur industry, particularly Prince Edward Island. To show just what this industry amounts to I might say that in 1935 we produced 190,000 silver fox pelts valued at 87,000,000. Of this total some 83,000,000 worth came from the little province of Prince Edward Island, between 81,000,000 and 82,000,000 worth from New Brunswick and the remainder from the rest of Canada. The objection of the fox fur producers is that while we have to pay a 50 per cent ad valorem duty if we send our fox furs to the United States, under this item they are permitted to ship furs into Canada free. In other words we are entirely shut out from the United States market while the fur producers of that country can send their furs to Canada without the payment of any duty.
In that connection I might also say that to-day the United States is the great competitor of the fox fur producers of Canada. Last year in that country they produced
160,000	pelts while we produced 190,000. They have our market in Canada free; they also compete with us in markets all over the world, and I understand that in no other country in the world is there a tariff against fox furs. That is what the fox fur producers are objecting to. A few years ago, Mr. Chairman, live foxes were shipped to the United States from Prince Edward Island and New Brunswick where we have the largest fox farm in the world, in the village of Salisbury. As soon as they had enough of our pure bred fox stock to form ranches of their own the United States imposed a 15 per cent duty against that pure bred stock, and I understand also that it was because of the representations made by the fox producers of Wisconsin and other western states that we were not given a reduction in the United States tariff on foxes and fox pelts entering that country. On behalf of the fox producers of the maritime provinces, as well as those in other parts of Canada, I feel that I am justified in protesting against this item.
A few moments ago the hon. member for Colchester-Hants (Mr. Purdy) said the people

of the maritime provinces were quite satisfied with the treaty, or words to that effect. I want to say, Mr. Chairman, that they are not satisfied with it. I repeat what I said here a few days ago; they are not satisfied. Ask the fishermen of Queens-Lunenburg; read your Nova Scotia newspapers, and you will find out how satisfied they are. As far as lumber is concerned, my hon. friend said that in 1930 our lumber was denied entry to the United States. That happened before the Conservative government came into power.
I did not say that.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: We are on furs just now.

The hon. gentleman referred to me in his remarks and I am just replying to him. However, as I said a moment ago, we are not satisfied with this treaty, and this is just another item in connection with which the people of the maritime provinces have been greatly prejudiced. It might be of interest to know the amount of furs that have been shipped into Canada from the United States. I find that the United States shipped fox furs into Canada in the following amounts:
1931		 $472,950
1932		 154,278
1933		 154,375
1934		 252,892
My understanding is these are inferior furs that cannot be sold in their own country, and having free access to our markets they send them in here to compete with our furs. Then again we are producing in this country on farms, and also catching wild, many mink. This item also comes under this tariff, and I believe there is a reduction from 15 per cent to 10 per cent.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No, this item is all free and has been free, coming from the United States into Canada. It is not changed at all.
Not otherwise provided?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No, fur skins of all kinds, not dressed in any manner. They have been free and continue free.

Well, that makes it all the worse. As far as undressed mink skins are concerned, the imports from the United States into Canada were as follows:
1931		 $338,379
1932		 116,306
1933		 71,642
1934		 217,778
This, I contend again, is in competition with our Canadian mink fur growers. Then take muskrat, a very important fur in Canada, and particularly in the maritime provinces. According to the figures of the bureau of statis-

Canada-U. S. Trade Agreement
tics the United States shipped into Canada muskrat skins as follows:
1931		 $1,065,018
1932		 742,763
1933		 345,053
1934		 1,069,381
I am protesting on behalf of the fur growers of my own district and other parts of the maritime provinces,

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
On this item I think I should put in a word for my own constituents who are silver fox producers. There is of course no doubt that the producers of foxes in Canada would have been delighted to secure free entry into the United States for fox furs, the same treatment as is accorded the furs of all other fur bearing animals. I assume my hon. friend would expect that any government negotiating an agreement of this kind would do its best to secure a concession in respect of an article of that description. But as to the seriousness of the situation as affecting our producers, I point out that our total exports of fox skins to all countries last year were $5,700,000, and we imported from the United States of that article $89,000 worth and exported to the United States
S197,000	worth. I think my hon. friend is correct in saying that certain low grades of skins come in, but the important thing for the fox producers of this country is export markets; for among the ten million people of Canada there certainly is not a sufficient number of potential silver fox buyers to sustain the industry that this country is capable of developing in that line. We are anxious to develop export markets for this commodity and have succeeded. The growth of this industry is quite remarkable; it is indeed an indication of the manner in which the people of Prince Edward Island have been able to build up a new industry adapted to the climatic conditions and the special situation of that province. It is a very valuable industry from the standpoint not only of foxes but of other fur bearing animals as well. When we see for instance that last year our total imports of furs of all kinds under this item were $2,600,000 and our total exports $14,800,000, it emphasizes the great importance to Canada still, notwithstanding the development of other industries, of Canada's original industry, that of producing furs. I may point out further that of that total our importations from the United States amounted to $1,700,000, whereas we exported to the United States S4,000,000 worth. I assure my hon. friend that this government is desirous of encouraging in every way the intelligent development of an industry potentially so valuable as this one, and will make
every effort to obtain and develop markets for its products.
The minister will not mind if I say it seems to me he has made a very strong argument why our furs should be admitted to the United States free on the same basis as theirs are admitted here.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Agreed.
But they have not accomplished that.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: They have not accomplished that.

We have heard a good deal about fox farming in the maritime provinces. It may surprise some hon. members to know that in Saskatchewan we do a lot of fox fanning. We brought a man from Prince Edward Island and he imported the foxes from that province, but he then did what we usually do in Saskatchewan-we improve things. He went out and won the championship of the world. And finally, Mr. Chairman, we are not asking for protection.
Like the minister, I was under the impression that the prior item had not been carried, although the chairman allowed the discussion of No. 601, to which the minister objected. On that item-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Which item?
No. 599, the one before.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: He ruled against me.
I think he was wrong. The minister said that the exports and imports were about equal, but as I recall it there is a handicap of ten per cent going into the United States on cowhides, bovine hides.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Bovine species, 10 per cent; all others free.
But they are free coming into Canada.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes, and they have always been free.

That is all right, but this is a case in which I think we ought to have got equality of treatment. Then about furs; the minister says wre are anxious to develop an export market, surely the United States ought to be a field where many people can buy the most valuable silver fox furs.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It is our second most valuable market now.
Still they have a duty against us, although they come in here free.

This being the last item, I am going to take the opportunity, Mr. Chairman, to compliment you; you make an excellent chairman. I am in order. The editorials sincerely compliment the government on this agreement, but the chairman who preceded you, sir, said the editorials were reflecting on this agreement. Order.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, may I say to my hon. friend I think the rule is that when a discussion is taking

place it is not permissible to read news items emanating from persons outside the house, and referring to anything said by a member or expressing any opinion on proceedings within the house. What my hon. friend is proposing to do is to read some newspaper articles from United States papers which are in the nature of editorial opinion relating to the subject under discussion here. If he is given that right I would have to be given that right, and I could find just as many articles that show the benefit of this agreement to the continent as a whole as he could find to support the contention he is making that the agreement is to the advantage of one particular country. It is to avoid the possibility of bringing in discussion from outside that the rule is there, and I do not think it should be violated.

Then I shall not read
the article. I think too much of the Prime Minister to oppose him in this regard.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Thank you.

And when I say I think
a lot of the Prime Minister, that is from my heart. The trend of all this United States newspaper comment is that this agreement will provide employment for the factories of the United States. I believe that. They say that the agreement at the same time will provide a home market for the American farmer. I believe that too, and that is what I would hope we shall get here, a home market for the Canadian farmer by increasing production in Canada.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Having read
the articles, Mr. Chairman, I may point out that what they say along the lines the hon. member has indicated may be said equally with respect to the effect of the agreement on Canada. The position, however, is a bit reversed. May I point out that what helps the Canadian farmer and other primary producers will help to make a home market here for the Canadian manufacturer. Conditions in Canada are going to be materially improved by virtue of the increased trade that will take place between the two countries. I could read many of the editorials which assert this-
I shall not object to the Prime Minister reading them. Go ahead; I think you should read them.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council

It would not
be in order. The editorials for the most part point out that this agreement will be mutually beneficial; that it breaks a hole in the wall of economic nationalism which has

says:
In the meantime, and pending the entry into force of the legislative changes foreshadowed in this note, the Canadian government are prepared as from the 1st January, 1936, to cancel the values for duty purposes, established under authority of section 43 of the Customs Act of Canada and now applicable to the undermentioned goods, the produce or manufacture of the United States, on importation into Canada: Meats, fresh, prepared' or preserved; eggs, frozen, desiccated, powdered, et cetera; loganberries, dried; slack cooperage stock; lime; doors of hardwood; women's and children's clothing; fabrics of cotton or of artificial silk; fringes, gimps and tassels; electric light fixtures; lamps and shades; roses, cut; canned asparagus; eggs in the shell; baby chicks; peas, dried; beans, dried; market poultry; iive stock; canned salmon; sugar of milk.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Purely as a matter of order, Mr. Chairman, and I am sure my hon. friend does not want to be out of order, we are on article III of the agreement. We have discussed the schedule mentioned in article III and we are now in the position of carrying article III. What my hon. friend is referring to really does not relate to article III at all. I shall have no objection at the proper time to discussing the point he raises, but it would be out of order to do so now. The rule is quite distinct that discussion in committee must be strictly relevant to the item under consideration, and I know my hon. friend does not want to follow the example of some others and wander far afield. I have no desire to avoid discussion on the point, but obviously there is a proper place for it.

It seems to me, with the greatest respect for my hon. friend's opinion, that this matter does relate to a large number of the items contained in schedule I, and



Canada-U. S. Trade Agreement
affects the rates of duties on these commodities entering Canada. Instead of dealing with it on each particular item it would only be fair and proper, when we are through with the schedule, to deal with it as it relates to the whole schedule. It does not relate to any one particular item. I should like to ask the minister when he thinks an opportunity for discussion would be given more appropriately than under schedule I?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The effect of the arbitrary valuations upon individual items was discussed when those items were before the committee. In connection with some of the items there was considerable discussion as to the effect of the removal of the arbitrary valuations which had been in force under the government of my hon. friends opposite. However, it seems to me that having lost the opportunity for what might be called a general discussion at that point, a further opportunity is given only when any action is taken by the government in a legislative way to implement the contents of the note dated November 15, 1935, addressed to the United States government. It was administrative action that was taken. My hon. friend read what it was. In no way did it affect the law. We undertook to remove certain fixed valuations as of a certain date. That promise has been implemented; the artificial valuations to which my hon. friend referred have been removed.

In discussing certain items we discussed the right to fix a valuation for duty purposes as there was a provision to that effect in connection with those items. The minister says "when any action is taken by the government," but action has been taken.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I said, when action is taken to propose an amendment to the law. What my hon. friend is discussing is an administrative action.

Item No. 12 on the order paper covers the second reading of Bill No. 11, to amend the Customs Act. This bill deals with the amendment of section 43. When this bill is before the house I shall be prepared to discuss the matter which the hon. member would like to discuss now. As a strict matter of order I suggest that that is when it should be discussed, rather than when we are dealing with a reciprocity agreement. That is not part of this reciprocity agreement. As Minister of National Revenue I cancelled a large number of the special valuations referring to the items in the list read by the hon. gentleman. We are introducing an amendment to section 43 and other sections of the
(Mr. Stewart,]
Customs Act and at that stage of our proceedings a discussion of the action of the Minister of National Revenue in cancelling these valuations would be strictly in order.

I would admit at once the contention of the Minister of National Revenue if it were not for the fact that this letter of November 15 has to all intents and purposes been made a part of the agreement. If it covered some action that was to be taken without reference to the agreement, if it were not a part of it and not for the purpose of implementing the provisions and understandings arrived at, then I would say the minister was correct. But this note is really a pari of the agreement, and I submit that the proper place to discuss it is when we are discussing the agreement. It has an effect upon schedule I, and we ought now to be given an opportunity of discussing its effect upon the schedule.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I submit that that procedure would be entirely out of order, for the reasons advanced by the Minister of National Revenue. The fact is that there is already notice of legislation upon the order paper. The only way in which this can be dealt with is by amending the specific statute, which amendment is being presented to parliament at as early a day as possible. It is a question which must be discussed in parliament, but there is a proper time and place for that discussion. In order to avoid confusion in dealing with these matters, I submit that this discussion is out of order.

It seems to me the Minister of Finance has missed the point. Perhaps I have not made myself clear. If it were a matter of legislation that was required and upon which no action had been taken, then his contention would be sound. Let me read again one paragraph of the letter, as follows:
In the meantime and pending the entry into force of the legislative changes foreshadowed in this note, the Canadian government are prepared as from the 1st January, 1936, to cancel the values for duty purposes, established under authority of section 43 of the Customs Act of Canada now applicable to the undermentioned goods, the produce or manufacture of the United States, on importation into Canada.
There is action taken; it is not action contemplated at all.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
That is the whole point. The existing law gives to any government the power to do or undo in connection with the matter to which my hon. friend refers. What comes before this parliament are the necessary

Canada-U. S. Trade Agreement
legislative changes, and these are covered by the bill already referred to. There is no legislative proposal before this committee dealing with section 43 of the Customs Act and the powers extended to the government thereunder. That necessary legislation is on the order paper and will come forward in due course. It comes partly in consequence of the undertaking given in the note to which my hon. friend refers, but surely it is a well known ruling that when notice of an amendment is on the order paper, when it is down for discussion by parliament at a future day, discussion cannot presently be entered upon in connection therewith when an entirely different matter is before the committee.

I am not anticipating discussion at all; I am inviting and contending for a discussion on an accomplished fact, just as this agreement itself is an accomplished fact. The discussion on this agreement has not been discussion anticipating proposed legislation; it has been a discussion upon something that has been done and that is now effective. It does not require any legislation to make it effective.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: May I say just this word? What the hon. member has read refers to what is a part of the government's general policy with respect to arbitrary valuations; it is not something peculiar to this agreement. He read from a letter which accompanied the agreement and which contained a statement indicating the government's general policy with respect to arbitrary valuations. It is not peculiar to this agreement; it is part of the general policy with respect to arbitrary valuations.
It applies to all intermediate tariff countries.

But a special undertaking is given with respect to this agreement.
Article III agreed to.
On article IV:
Articles the growth, produce or manufacture of Canada, enumerated and described in schedule II annexed to this agreement, shall, on their importation into the "United States of America, be exempt from ordinary customs duties in excess of those set forth and provided for in the said schedule. The said articles shall also be exempt from all other duties, taxes, fees, charges, or exactions, imposed on or in connection with importation, in excess of those imposed on the day of the signature of this agreement or required to be imposed thereafter under laws of the United States of America in force on the day of the signature of this agreement.
Schedule II and the notes included therein shall have full force and effect as integral parts of this agreement.

Before we go into the schedules I should like to say this to my right hon. friend. It seems to me that in making this arrangement with the United States he has very much overlooked the condition of their tariff at the present time. While the right hon. gentleman was in office the United States in 1922 passed the Fordney-McCumber tariff, the rates of which were very high, higher than in any tariff act previously passed by that country. At that time it was felt in Canada that those rates imposed by the United States were unfair and that they were higher than they ought to be considering that we were such good neighbours. Those increased duties were imposed upon products subject to duty under previous tariffs, but higher rates were provided over a wide range of commodities. For instance, the Fordney-McCumber tariff imposed high rates on certain classes of fish previously free, and those high duties have served adversely to affect our fisheries. My right hon. friend will say that the trade between Canada and the United States increased after the imposition of the Fordney-McCumber tariff. That is quite true. But we must remember that those were years when there was a good deal of excitement throughout the world, prices went up and trade increased, but the whole world suffered the reaction in 1929. But not content with that, the United States in 1930, before my right hon. friend went out of office, passed the Hawley-Smoot tariff, and the increases made in that tariff were such as to lead many people to regard the previous rates as comparatively low indeed. Never before has any country imposed a tariff on the scale of the Hawley-Smoot tariff; indeed, the rates they put into force were prohibitive on a great many of our exports, and the consequence was that the volume of those exports declined materially during the next few years.
What has happened in this instance? My right hon. friend went to Washington and put through this agreement, which he is fond of declaring to be the same as the one we had in mind, though that statement has been contradicted by my leader. However, I would call his attention to this fact. Looking over these rates in schedule II and comparing them with the rates previously in force in the United States, both under the Hawley-Smoot tariff and under the Fordney-McCumber tariff, I find that in most instances the concessions which he has obtained from the United States are so small that even now under this agreement the rates are higher than they were under the Fordney-McCumber tariff. In other words, the United States imposed extreme rates in the Hawley-Smoot tariff, and then my right hon. friend goes to Washington and

Canada-U. S. 'Trade Agreement
enters into an agreement and they say, "We will give you these concessions." And what are they? They are in most instances-the new rates he has obtained-higher than the rates were under the high Fordney-McCumber tariff. I will not labour that point because it has been fully discussed in the house; but I must say that I was surprised to see what the situation was when I looked over these rates.
Let us take milk and cream, items that are of interest to the whole country; certainly they are of interest to the people in my constituency as well as to every other farming community. What is the situation? Under this new tariff arrangement my right hon. friend has obtained a rate of 35 cents a gallon. Under the Hawley-Smoot tariff it was 56^y cents a gallon, and the reduction looks like a large one. But under the Fordney-McCumber tariff it was only 20 cents, and that tariff when it was put into force was regarded as very high, higher than any other tariff they had ever had in the United States. Of what use is the concession to us when the rate on cream is left at 35 cents, seeing that it was 20 cents under the Fordney-McCumber tariff? It is worse than the Fordney-McCumber tariff.
I do not find milk mentioned in the agreement at all. Under the Fordney-McCumber tariff it was 2i cents a gallon, and the present rate is 61 cents. The right hon. gentleman has not succeeded in getting any concession on this very important item. However, I will not labour all this. I simply say as a business man, looking over the figures, that I am astonished to find that these rates which the United States has now given Canada are in most cases higher than under the Fordney-McCumber tariff, which was at that time the highest tariff ever put into force there.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Everything
my right hon. friend has said about the Fordney-McCumber tariff is equally true with respect to the intermediate tariff on our side. We are giving the United States the intermediate tariff but it is entirely different from the intermediate tariff that existed at the time to which he refers. As he knows, since the government of which he was a member came into office it busied itself every year in raising the general tariff and in jacking up the intermediate tariff to a point where on many items it was scarcely distinguishable from the general tariff. The result is that in giving the United States to-day the benefit of the intermediate tariff Canada does not begin to concede what would have been given in the intermediate as it was in 1930. It is equally true, as my right hon. friend has said, that had the tariff remained where it was some
lSir George Perley.]
years ago, so far as the United States is concerned, the concessions now granted would be greater than they are. But surely that is not an argument against obtaining the benefit of as large a reduction as possible in a tariff that had become practically prohibitive, so as to secure a considerable entry into the American market for Canadian produce and goods.
My right hon. friend has taken care to pick out here and there individual items on which as large concessions as he had wished for, have not been obtained. He has referred to milk. I believe that if his government had begun negotiations earlier than they did, a substantial reduction on milk might have been secured. As he knows, the longer the negotiations were deferred, and the nearer the time of negotiating approached the assembly of congress and a presidential election in the United States, the more difficult it was to obtain concessions as great as they otherwise might have been. As to the concessions not being as great as they might have been, that is in no way the fault of the present administration. It is in very considerable measure the result of the inaction in negotiating of our predecessors in office. When the committee comes to examine, as I hope it will examine in detail these various items, it will find that the concessions obtained are very considerable. When my right hon. friend referred to the Fordney-McCumber tariff he did not refer to lumber, but he will recall that under the Fordney-McCumber tariff, lumber, together with many other commodities, was not in the position to which he has referred. However, I will not take up the time of the committee now. I think my right hon. friend will be answered in full if we go through schedule II item by item, as we did schedule I. The committee will then get an appreciation of the reciprocal nature of the agreement as a whole, and of what has been obtained in the way of concessions by Canada upon articles going into the United States as compared with the concessions we have given to the United States upon commodities coming into Canada.
Sir GEORGF. PERLEY: With some parts of the remarks of my right hon. friend the Prime Minister I quite agree. The question whether the late government was responsible for this has already been discussed ad nauseam; the right hon. gentleman reiterates it, but it has been explained fully that the late government were unable to go on with this negotiation any faster than they did. speechtext: My right hon. friend knows there is still to be a bill based on the resolution now before the house, and when the bill is introduced there will be an opportunity at different stages of the bill to ask questions.

In committee

There is one statement
of the Prime Minister in connection with the imposition of duties by the late government which I think requires a little attention and a little development in addition to what it has received at the hands of the hon. member for Argenteuil (Sir George Perley). He says the duties were raised. Undoubtedly they were, and he knows the reason; he has been told and this house has been told. The general tariff was raised and the intermediate tariff was raised, as he says, but I suggest to him that an examination will show the increases were not as serious as he indicates; the increases in the tariff itself were not very extensive.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Oh yes, they were.

The complaint all along has been the valuation for duty purposes rather than the increase in the tariff as such. In the last budget there were reductions on a very substantial number of items in the intermediate tariff and the general tariff.

I would just like to point out to the hon. member for Leeds (Mr. Stewart) and the hon. member for Argenteuil (Sir George Perley) that in 1930 they and their leader distinctly told the people of Canada that the reason we were suffering at that time was that we were doing too much business for the United States.
Not too much business with the United States.

They said that in the previous year $900,000,000 worth of goods came in from that great country and $800,000,000 of exports had gone out, and that that was the cause of our troubles at that time. The government of the day pledged themselves to see that that condition was done away with, that that trade should be killed, and they did kill it. They adopted weapon; in order to kill that trade. But let me poim out that the proportions of the trade remainec the same. At the bottom of the depressior we were still doing about the same proportior of business with the United States that wc were doing in 1930, and we are doing it to-day; because apparently the percentages do not change very much, it is only the volume that changes with these kinds of restrictions. The hon. member for Leeds says that last yeai very substantial reductions in tariffs were made. It is true that reductions were made in the last year or two, because even the late government came to its senses in some slight degree, like a man who has had a severe attack of certain troubles and, beginning to recover from them, regains his senses. The government which had put this country down from the position in which it stood economically in 1930 to the position it occupied in 1932 naturally wanted to help to bring about recovery, and began to make reductions of tariffs from the unparalleled height which they had reached, although that slight lopping off did not bring them down to the position they were in in 1930 and to where they should be in 1936 or 1937 at the latest. But the action taken to keep our trade from the United States was premeditated. Because goods could not come in from the United States the people of this country were not able to enjoy them and were not able to get payment for the goods they shipped to the United States and other markets; for the only way they could be paid for goods sent out was to bring goods in, and the door was slammed in the face of other nations by the late government. I am not blaming that government for doing it. They promised us they would do it and they did it, by a high tariff, by special valuations for duty purposes, by dump duties, by excise and the other devices they adopted; and it is to clear the channel of these obstructions that we are now engaged in this work.
Mr. STEWART; The hon. member for Melfort (Mr. McLean) was good enough to say that the government showed some signs

Canada-U. S. Trade Agreement
of repentance. I have not detected any in his attitude either towards the late government or towards the policy of protection.
My attitude has not been proven wrong yet.
It has, but you do not realize it.

He says that the object of the late government's action was to kill trade with the United States. That is not at all a fair statement; I think that upon reflection hon. members will agree with me. The fact is that there was a very heavy adverse balance of trade, and because of that the financial credit of Canada was in difficulties. Some action was necessary to change the situation, because we could not go on meeting that adverse balance year after year, increasing the deficit.
Why not?

Oh well, let the hon. member ask some of his economist friends; they will tell him very quickly. That was the reason for the action of the late government. It was not for the purpose of killing trade. No intelligent person would have any such intention.
They certainly did it.
No. World trade shrank. It shrank in every country in the world. It shrank in free trade countries, if you can find one. It shrank in Spain, in Germany, in Great Britain, everywhere.
What purpose had your government in putting on the restrictions that they put on if it was not to limit trade?
To try and keep a few jobs for Canadians.
The restrictions put on trade by Canada were insignificant in comparison with the restrictions put against her in other countries.
Even though that is true, why were they put on?
In the interests of Canadian citizens, Canadian workers. In the interests of my hon. friend himself.
To further trade or stop trade with other countries?
No, not to stop trade at all.
Did it increase trade?

I want to put on the record two thoughts in connection with the dis-

cussion concerning this schedule of tariff rates on Canadian goods entering the United States. I am not in a position to follow hon. gentlemen opposite in the comparisons they are making between the rates under this agreement and the rates that existed under some previous United States tariff, but I am in a position to make a comparison between the actual living conditions, now and prior to the agreement, of the people engaged in the industries affected by the rates brought about as a result of this agreement with the United States, and that comparison between the actual living conditions of the people engaged in lumbering, cattle raising and certain other industries is utterly to the advantage of the people of Canada. I am not going to try to follow my hon. friends in their doctrinal discussion concerning a comparison of rates, but if hon. members will consult their own constituents engaged in the industries affected bs' this agreement they will find that no matter what may be the comparison of rates, a comparison of living conditions since January 1, and those previously prevailing, and of the hopes of the people for the next few years, is entirely to the advantage of Canada. After all it is the living conditions of the people that count; I believe the people of Canada are interested in that question in the discussion of tariff agreements.
The second thought I wish to present is this: During the full dress debate in connection with this reciprocity agreement hon. gentlemen opposite told us that because we were allowing trade channels to be opened north and south and because we were going to trade with the United States, we were going to make Canada part and parcel of the American union of states, that we were to become a new state of the union. If that is a real, living fear within their minds in regard to this reciprocity agreement I want to ask why they are so anxious to show the people of Canada that the Prime Minister did not obtain from the United States tariff rates sufficiently low to enable more Canadian products to go to that country, so that the flow of trade north and south would be even greater than it is going to be under this agreement. If they are afraid that the flow of trade, by becoming greater, will make Canada a part of the American union, why are they so annoyed because we are not making that flow even larger by securing greater concessions from the United States?
Mr. MaeINNIS: Mr. Chairman, the members of this group have not said very much during the long discussion on this question,

Canada-U. S. Trade Agreement
and it seems to me that a great deal of the discussion has been very unreal as far as the actual facts and conditions are concerned. My hon. friends opposite have been accusing the present opposition, when in power, of destroying trade. I do not think there is anything to that kind of talk. The world depression put an end to trade.
What made the depression?
My hon. friend should ask the government that was in office when the depression began.
I just want to tell my hon. friend that the depression did not begin in Canada until after the government changed.
Just a moment; I have the floor, and I will tell my hon. friend that the government was defeated because the depression began before they went to the country.
They were defeated because my hon. friend's friends and hon. gentlemen opposite promised to make the people of Canada rich, comfortable and happy, and then did not keep that promise.
Quite so; I agree that they made that promise.
Your friends.

Just a moment; keep quiet. When my hon. friend had the floor I did not interrupt him. The statements made by the former government in 1930 would not have had much effect on the people of this country if the people had not been in difficulty at that time. That is correct.
No, no.

Yes, of course that is
correct. It was because the Liberal government of 1930 would not even admit that there was a problem confronting the people of Canada that the government was defeated. I am not going to say that from 1930 to 1935 the Conservative government did very much to overcome the depression, because they did not. However, it should be noted that things began to improve while they were in office,, and possibly they will continue to improve for some time to come. But the point that we should remember is that the conditions that brought about the depression of 1930 are still with us and will bring about another depression within a few years, regardless of which party is in office.
I do not believe that the evils that have been suggested by the opposition are going
to befall the country just because of this agreement. Neither am I going to agree that the great benefits the government say will accrue to the country will come about. However, that is no reason why we should oppose this agreement, and we are not opposing it. We supported the government on the agreement, and we will have to judge the benefits of this treaty not from the way it may affect any one industry in particular but from the way it may affect economic conditions in this country as a whole. We cannot judge that within a few months; it will take some little time to find out whether or not the agreement is going to be beneficial.
I am in favour of the agreement, particularly because it is a step towards cooperation. We have started to cooperate with the government of the United States for the purpose of reducing tariffs and making it easier for goods to flow from this country into the United States and from the United States into this country. If we can even begin to cooperate I think perhaps the benefits of cooperation may become so manifest in a very short time that we shall continue to do so on a very much larger scale. So I suggest that we get through with this agreement, or the remainder of it, with a little less discussion than we have had heretofore. It will go through in any case, and we- can only judge of its benefits or otherwise as time goes on. Regardless of what may happen during the course of this agreement the government will have a great many other difficulties to overcome before it can bring prosperity to this country on such a scale that there will be any appreciable effect on the economic life of our people.

Item 11 is paragraph 11 of the United States Tariff Act of 1930. It appears as the next item in schedule II. Canada, however, obtains the treatment accorded any other nation with which the United States has an agreement. There are many items in the United States tariff which are not included in schedule II and on which the United States has granted concessions in either of the agreements it has made. I think therefore, in order to bring out just what Canada has obtained by way of concessions, as a result of the most-favoured nation provision of the agreement this is an appropriate time to place on Hansard particulars of the benefits accruing through these

Canada-U. S. Trade Agreement
other agreements and which do not appear in this schedule. A statement has been presented to the house in the form of a white paper giving these particulars. I should like to point out, for example, that Canada obtains, by virtue of the United States having an agreement with the Netherlands, a reduction on amyl alcohol from 6 cents to 4 cents per pound, on fusel oil from 6 cents to 4 cents per pound, on laundry sour from 25 per cent to 15 per cent, on ammonium silicofluoride from 25 to 15 per cent, on Haarlem oil from 25 to 15 per cent. These all come under an agreement the United States has with the Netherlands, of which Canada gets the benefit.
Then arising out of the agreement of the United States with Belgium, on aluminum sulphate there is a change in the rate from 0-2 cents or 0-375 cents per pound to 0-2 cents, on copaiba balsam, natural and uncompounded, and not containing alcohol, from 10 per cent to 5 per cent ad valorem through an agreement which the United States has with Brazil. On tolu balsam, natural and uncompounded, and not containing alcohol, there is a reduction from 10 to 5 per cent by virtue of an agreement which the United States has with Colombia.
The items I have referred to are in paragraphs 4, 5, 6 and 10 of the United States tariff. The next item we come to is No. 11, the one the minister has in hand at the moment.

I regret to say that I cannot give those figures; we do not have them available.

Apparently they are
trifling.

This is a new matter. We are only now getting the benefit of these favoured nation agreements that the United States have with the other countries. My hon. friend will realize no doubt that it would be quite an undertaking to get all these figures now.
I would think so, on these items.
They are, however, being announced week by week.

Perhaps we could get the
figures on some items.
If I have the information I shall be glad to give it.

I think that ought to be done. The Prime Minister has read a list of items on which we get these concessions, as if they were of some value. Now, are they of any value to this country? That is what we would like to know.

There naturally arises, I am sure, in the mind of every member of the committee, the same question that was suggested by the hon. member for Moose Jaw (Mr. Ross), that we should, where possible have the amount of our exports of these articles to the United States. From my knowledge I would say offhand that, with a few exceptions such as flavouring extracts, we do not produce any of these articles. Many of the other items sound very strange to me, so far as Canadian production is concerned. Our trade figures are comprehensive and are given very much in detail, so surely we ought to be able to get some estimate of what our exports of these articles are, and of whether these new duties are going to be of any advantage to us at all.

It must be quite apparent that the value of these concessions which we receive by having favoured nation treatment extended to us by the United States must necessarily be to some extent a matter of experience in the future to determine. As to the amount of business we are now doing in these commodities with other countries the figures are not available at the moment, but when these items come up again in committee on the bill it may be possible to supply my hon. friend with details on some of the more substantial items in the list.

I am not so much
interested in the business we are doing in these commodities with other countries as I am in knowing whether we produce any of these goods.

As a result of this trade agreement the benefit of favoured nation treatment is given to us the same as to these other countries by the United States, and I understood my hon. friend to say that he would like to know what exports we were already making to these other countries.
No; to the United States.
We have not that information at hand.
We should like to know whether we produce these commodities in Canada.
Some of" them we do.

I notice that the duties on cobalt oxide, cobalt sulphate and many other items are given at so much per pound. The duty on cobalt oxide, for instance, is 10 cents per pound and on cobalt sulphate, 5 cents per pound. But how does that work out as a percentage? What is the value of cobalt

oxide per pound? If we knew that, we would have some idea of what the concession amounts to and of the prospect of obtaining additional trade with the United States, which at least we hope that we shall get.
On the basis of 1932 exports the duty on cobalt oxide would be 20 per cent ad valorem.
Do I understand that the value of cobalt oxide is about 50 cents per pound?
At that time it was.
