speakeroldname: Mr. J. S. WOODSWORTH (Winnipeg North Centre):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, When this bill was last under discussion I was pointing out that the government could not escape responsibility for this measure. It is true that it is a private bill, but the government, speaking through the Secretary of State (Mr. Rinfret), has seen fit to try to advance this bill, suggesting that it should be allowed to pass second
reading and go to a committee. Year after year we have had commissions and committees of this house and of the senate dealing with the Civil Service Act. Now it would seem as if an attempt is being made to introduce fundamental changes in the act by a sort of back-door method. If the government want to change the Civil Service Act I suggest that they should bring about that change in a recognized way, themselves definitely taking the responsibility of bringing forward a bill, or perhaps themselves setting up a committee to go once more into the question. But I do object to a private member introducing a bill of this kind, having such far-reaching effects, and the house being expected to pass it through on second reading, that is to give assent to the principle underlying the bill. I would appeal to the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) himself, if he were in his seat, himself a former civil servant, that he should not in any way countenance the passing of a bill of this sort. I could not but think of those brave words that the Prime Minister uttered on the night of the election, and that he repeated in the house in one of his first speeches this session.
To-day's victory is a victory for democracy.
Is that going to be watered down to mean that a Liberal victory was simply a victory for reaction and the setting aside of the Civil Service Act, which has been in existence for so long, and introducing once more the patronage system? He said further:
It constitutes a great deliverance; a deliverance of the people from one-man government, irom mistaken policies, and from autocratic leadership. It is a triumph for broad principles and policies, as against promises and pledges recklessly and extravagantly made for the sole purpose of winning an election.
Brave words these; yet within a few months after they were uttered; within a few weeks after the opening of this parliament, we have the Liberal party with all its liberal traditions asking this house to further a measure which is essentially a return to patronage.
In that notable speech the Prime Minister further said:
It is clear evidence of the desire of the people of Canada to maintain high standards in Canadian public life, and to enjoy a tone in the discussion of public affairs wholly different from that to which, both in and out of parliament, they have became accustomed during the past five years.

On a point of order, Mr. Speaker, I think the hon. gentleman is certainly out of order in quoting from a previous debate in the present session.

Civil Service Act

I think the point taken by the hon. member for Lake Centre is quite in order. I do not think the hon. member has a right to quote from a previous debate. I refer to Beauchesne's Parliamentary Rules and Forms, page 95, Standing Order 41:
...a member, while speaking, must not: _
(a) refer to any debate of the same session on any question not then under discussion.
Besides being set down in the standing order the rule has been sanctioned by usage in both England and Canada, that an hon. member while speaking must not refer to any debate of the same session on any question not then under discussion.
I point out that I am referring to a public speech made by the Prime Minister on the night of the election.
But it was incorporated in a debate in the house.

If the Prime Minister undertakes in the course of a debate to quote from the Bible surely that does not mean that we are forever precluded during the rest of the session from quoting the Bible in this assembly.
Order.
I suggest that I am quite in order in quoting from a speech of the Prime Minister made outside this house.
Go ahead.
I think the Prime Minister would not deny me that right.
The rule is very clear; it is distinctly stated that it is not in order to quote from a previous debate in the same session, and that is what the hon. gentleman is now attempting to do.
I think the hon. member should abide by the rules and the decision I have given.
I am abiding by the rules of this house, but I submit that the rules do not prevent my quoting from a speech made by the Prime Minister outside this house on October 14, last.
The hon. gentleman is quoting from Hansard the report of a previous debate in the present session.

I do not know that I am in order in speaking after Your Honour has rendered a decision, but the rules of the house are clear that hon. members may not quote from a previous debate. The

hon. member now has Hansard of this session and he is quoting from a previous debate during this session. The hon. gentleman is not quoting from a speech delivered outside the house; he is quoting from the Hansard report of the Prime Minister's speech made during this session.
Does the hon. member appeal from the ruling? I thought I had rendered my decision.
I am not going to take the time of the house to challenge Your Honour's ruling, but I protest against it.
Order. I rendered my decision, which is in accordance with decisions rendered in many other cases.
I say that I am not going to challenge Your Honour's ruling; all I want to do is to protest against it.
The hon. member will be named.

Well, then I will be named. The hon. member is not going to frighten me by suggesting that. If this Liberal government is going to expel a member for quoting from a speech made outside this house, then I am quite willing to walk out.
I desire in the name of the government to say that the government have taken no part in this little discussion.
I hope the government are not siding with the Speaker in this instance in preventing the quotation from a speech made outside the house.
Order.
Mr. Speaker having given his ruling, I am precluded from giving my own opinion, but I desire to say again that the government have taken no part in the discussion of this point of order.

speechtext: The government assume responsibility.

You are not far from the truth in doing so.

Coming back to the question of the civil service, I said that I was appealing to the Prime Minister and the Liberal government to live up to the ideals that have been set before us as the ideals of Liberalism. I would appeal to some of the members of the government. I spoke the other night with regard to the Minister of

Civil Service Act
Immigration (Mr. Crerar) who, if I remember aright, came down here many years ago pledged to the ideal of a civil service commission rather than patronage. I would appeal to the Postmaster General (Mr. Elliott) whether he approves a return to patronage. I would appeal to the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Euler), whom I have known in this house for a good many years. I would appeal to some of the newer members of the cabinet, to the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Ilsley) and the Minister of Labour (Mr. Rogers), who do not happen to be in their seats at the moment. I can hardly conceive that they will sanction a retrograde measure of this kind. We are told that we must have cabinet solidarity, but I cannot believe that the cabinet is united in a desire to advance a measure of this sort. I would appeal also to the western members. Did they come down to this house pledged to anything of a patronage nature? I would remind the Liberals that although they are here in such large numbers their victory was not quite so sweeping as one might imagine. In 1930 the Liberals polled 46.2 per cent of the total vote, and in 1935 they polled only 46.8 per cent of the whole vote. So it was not a very sweeping victory when you put it in that way.
Mr. CHEyRIER (Ottawa):	What has
that to do with the bill under discussion?
I warn the Liberals-
Warn yourself.

I warn the Liberals that if they put through measures of this kind the whole country west of the lakes is going to revolt.
I would point out to the new members on the other side of the house that although the gov eminent, speaking through the Secretary of State, seems willing to advance this bill, it is really a private measure. speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Why this violent outburst?
Mr. W'OODSWORTH: I say that the government, speaking through the Secretary of State, asked us to pass the second reading of this bill.
I made it very plain that I did not want to commit the house to the bill, but that the bill might go to a committee for study purposes. I said that I stood by the merit system.

Not even the Secretary of State can alter the fundamental rules of this house, and one of its fundamental rules is that the principle of a bill is decided on its second reading. We are deciding that principle now, and not even the Secretary of State can set that rule aside. If we approve the principle of this bill by voting for its second reading for study purposes or for any other plausible reason we are advancing the bill by one stage. I would say -to the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe) what I said before he came in, that the government cannot escape responsibility for advocating a. measure of this kind.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: The government does not advocate the measure.
Does the government speak through the Secretary of State?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Even the Secretary of State has a right to make a, suggestion to the house.

But surely he
makes it as a member of the government.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: My hon. friend breaks into an outburst which is absolutely unnecessary and unjustified.

Anything the Secretary of State suggests, he suggests as a member of the government, and the government is to that extent helping to advance this bill.
I would ask, Mr. Speaker, whether, alter all, patronage is such a great party asset. Members on the government side are pestered to
Civil Service Act

death by job hunters, and I need not remind them of what they know only too well, that for every man who gets a job through patronage ten men are disappointed. To-day there are not enough jobs to go round.
We know that.

Why seek to extend the area of patronage under those circumstances? Perhaps I might give away a little secret. I myself have always thought that one of the reasons, among others, why I have been elected was that I do not control any patronage. I do not think it is an asset to a member that he is able to give out a few odd jobs.
Patronage, I take it, is nothing less than a national vice; it is thinly veiled bribery. The social credit people to my left have sometimes been charged with offering a twenty-five dollars a month bribe. Be that as it may, what about the practice of taking care of one's political friends at the public expense? In China what is known as "squeeze" is held largely responsible for the weaknesses of a great nation. Are we to introduce something of the same kind here in Canada, and extend it right and left? Make no mistake, this bill is a return to patronage on a large scale, and anyone who seeks to advance this bill a further stage is in my judgment lending himself to a return to patronage.
What sort of efficiency, may I ask, is to be expected in the public service if there is no security at all and if there is no certitude that merit will be rewarded? What sort of efficiency can we expect if the idea prevails that a man's advancement will depend upon the whim of his political superior? It is bad enough that we cannot have even a barber in the House of Commons unless he is on the right side politically. Even the Free Press a few weeks ago had quite a satire on that. One has to be a Liberal, forsooth, nowadays in order to be a barber in the House of Commons, and yet the barber has to deal faithfully with every man who sits in his chair, be he a Liberal or a Conservative. That may be all very well, if you like, for barbers or messengers, but what about people occupying responsible positions? We have large numbers of scientists and other professional men occupying high positions in this country. Are we to say to men in the [DOT]outside service that they must be of the right political colour, wear a certain political badge, in order to be promoted? Are we going to say to those of a similar class outside that they cannot even be appointed to the civil service unless they are of the right political colour? If that is the case, I think it is indeed a deplorable situation. We are trying to teach

our boys in school that if they work hard and faithfully at their tasks they are fairly well assured of being able to get on in the world. But if measures of this kind are to become the law, I suggest that we shall have to alter that kind of teaching and tell them that they will have to do a lot of bootlicking, wear political badges and be subservient and then possibly they may get advancement in the public service. Is that the position we are coming to in Canada?
I remember several years ago, long before I entered parliament, going in to see the head of a department of one of the provincial governments, a man whom I had known for some years. He called me into his office. He had rather an important position, and I congratulated him upon it. He looked through the glass doors out over a great room filled with clerks. "Well," he said, "Mr. Woodsworth, I am not quite so sure about it. What can I do with a staff like that? Almost every day," he said, "the minister or somebody else sends a letter down to me, asking if I can make room for so and so, and I have to try and make room for him. I have undoubtedly," he said, "a great task and a great opportunity, but I am handicapped in having continually loaded upon me people who are not efficient."
Where was that?
In a department of one of the provincial governments. It happened some years ago.
In what province?

It is immaterial. The hon. gentleman will not doubt my word. I have used that simply as an illustration. My friend said that it was almost impossible for him to obtain efficiency in that department so long as he was handicapped by patronage of that kind. I suggest here to-night that we cannot very well hope to have efficiency in our civil service if we return to patronage of this sort.
Let me read a section of this bill which really contains the principle:
The outside service shall be excluded from the operation of this act, and the governor in council may make regulations for the control and direction, organization, classification and compensation, appointments to and general conditions of the outside service.
As I stated before, if the outside service is to be taken out from under the Civil Service Act, there is no reason why the same treatment should not be accorded to the inside service. When I made that statement the other evening the mover of this bill said,

Civil Service Act
"Hear, hear." He is in sympathy with that idea. In his judgment this is simply a forerunner of more "advanced" legislation along this line; I should put it rather more "retrograde" legislation. The present act contains this section in connection with promotions:
Promotion is a change from one class to another class with a higher maximum compensation, and vacancies shall be filled, as far as is consistent with the best interests of the civil service, by promotion.
There is no such principle contained in this bill. The section continues:
Promotions shall be made for merit by the commission upon such examination, reports, tests, records, ratings or recommendations as the commission may by regulation prescribe.
There is nothing in this bill to suggest that that principle is to be applied. The matter is to be left entirely to the discretion of the minister in charge. I am quite willing to admit, as I did the other evening, that there may be some room for improvement in the Civil Service Act and in the procedure by which appointments and promotions are made. If that is so, let the government introduce suitable legislation at this session and we will support to the utmost the changes necessary to make our civil service efficient. It is not necessary to-night to quote the members of the government against themselves. I plead with them that they refuse to consider the advancing of a retrograde measure of this kind.

Mr. Speaker, I congratulate the leader of the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation (Mr. Woodsworth) upon the splendid St. Patrick's day speech which he has just made. I would remind him that when a man talks loudly, as he has done, there is generally a fight in sight. I congratulate him upon the way in which he is celebrating St. Patrick's day. I agree with him in some respects, but I would remind hon. members on this side of the house that all the reformers are not to be found on one side of the chamber. I congratulate the introducer of this bill (Mr. Boulanger), because I think its introduction will lead to some reforms. It is stated that certain abuses have cropped up in the civil service. While I cannot say that I have actually seen any in my dealings with the service, I must say that I have seen signs of abuse. I do not think examinations should be held when a charwoman or cleaner is to be appointed to the public service. I think it is asking the examiners to do an impossible task when you ask them to pick out one woman from many who will make a better sweeper than the rest. I do not think
our civil service should have to stoop to that sort of thing, but I think it should aim to be more like the imperial civil service. To my mind that service is far above anything we have on this continent.
The intention of this bill is to give preference to the Canadian returned men. The Canadian returned soldier thinks that a man who left our shores to fight under the Canadian and British flags should have a preference over the man who fought for some other country. I believe the government would be well advised to take this feature of the bill into consideration. I do not want it thought that I am in any way advocating war, because I am utterly opposed to war. I do not think the civil service should be confined to Ottawa. Ottawa is a great city and there are many fine people residing here, but to me it will have to take second place to Fort William. I think the superintendent of a post office in another city should rate the same as a postmaster in Ottawa. I was going to say the same as the Postmaster General, but perhaps that would be asking too much. These superintendents should have equal rights and protection.
I believe that the government, no matter what party may be in power, should get as far away from patronage as is possible. To me patronage is the curse of politics today and the less we have of it, the better we will be. You cannot free yourself entirely from patronage until you get absolute honesty and unselfishness and I have as yet seen no signs of these qualities in any party in this house. Until you have absolute honesty, unselfishness and love, patronage will creep into the service, as it is creeping into even the civil service.

Mr. Speaker, surely this is a measure that can be discussed in this house with calmness. I must say that I was surprised at the suggestion made the other evening by the Secretary of State (Mr. Rinfret) that this bill should be given its second reading. It is quite true that he made it perfectly clear that he made this suggestion in order that the bill might be studied in committee. I am quite certain that the government is not behind this bill, but when a bill receives second reading it means that its principle is endorsed by the house. I think the Secretary of State erred in making the suggestion which he did, for he cannot alter the well recognized rule that second reading carries with it the endorsement of the bill. That being so, I am certainly opposed to the second reading of this bill. I have great
Civil Service Act

respect and admiration, for the hon. member for Bellechasse (Mr. Boulanger). I enjoyed the clever and charming manner in which he presented this bill to the house. He elaborated those sections of his bill which commended themselves generally to the house and he said as little as possible about those sections that did not.
He is a lawyer.

And a very good one.
While I approve entirely of the hon. member for Bellechasse in his private capacity, I do not approve the bill he is proposing to this house. Why should we send this bill to a committee? The passing of the bill on second reading endorses the principle of it, and if we are opposed to the principle we ought not to give the bill second reading.
Admittedly there are many defects in our civil service system and there are many respects in which the Civil Service Act ought to be amended. Indeed, I have heard it suggested -and I believe there is some truth in the suggestion-that the Civil Service Act when it was adopted in 1920 had rather peculiar and disastrous consequences. Prior to the passing of the act in 1920 the Tory government then in power had filled the civil service with Tory appointments, and then they passed the Civil Service Act which had the effect of clamping the act on the service as it then was, so that the civil service was made a self-perpetuating Tory machine, if a machine may be termed self-perpetuating.
The key to the civil service system is the rating board, and succeeding governments, one after another, have tried to obtain control of the key positions in the service, so that they might use these key positions for their own particular purposes, in view of the fact that the rating board is really the heart of the civil service system. If the rating board is fairly constituted and if the chairman of the rating board is a fair-minded man, no one can take any objection to the board or the appointments that are made. But if the chairman of the rating board is partisan and if the rating board is a partisan body, then we do not have a merit system, for if the chairman of the rating board is partisan and not a fair-minded man. he is anxious to see that the person whom ne favours from a political point of view rates at the top of the list. Then the rating board forwards its report which is dealt with by the authorities of the commission at Ottawa. Surely an effort should be made throughout the system to find proper men in the various departments to constitute these
(Mr. Thorson.l
rating boards and to select, when we do select men for key positions in the service, fair-minded men who will make their recommendations upon a real basis of merit and not upon any partisan basis as is frequently the case under the system as it exists to-day.
I would have no serious objection to the whole Civil Service Act being sent to a committee for investigation and study, both of the act itself and of the entire system, with a view not to weakening the act or to weakening the system, but to strengthening the system by studying the defects of the act. There are a number of serious defects in the Civil Service Act, but there is one in particular which I should like to bring to the attention of the house. There is in the act no provision at all for reinstatement of employees who have been dismissed from the civil service. It matters not that they have been wrongfully dismissed; it matters not that they have been dismissed in error, no provision is contained in the Civil Service Act for the reinstatement of employees in the civil service who have been forced to leave that service either through injustice or in error. The provisions with regard to reinstatement were deliberately left out of the act so that governments might use that as an excuse for not putting men back into the service even though they had been improperly dismissed. I have known cases where men have been improperly dismissed, but when it was desired to remedy the injustice it was found that these men could not enter the service, on the ground that they had exceeded the age limit and were therefore no longer eligible to enter the service, or if they wanted to get back into the service, they had to start at the beginning; they could not return to the service in the positions where they had left off or at the rating they had when dismissed. That is unfair; that is unsound; and if it is proposed to improve the Civil Service Act and to amend it in respects that require amendment, it would be much better to give some thought and attention to those respects in which the act is defective and requires amendment than to destroy those portions of the act which, while not perfect, have yet brought about a better state of affairs than existed previously. I would strongly urge that those who are giving thought and attention to our civil service should take this matter in hand with a view to correcting a very serious defect in the Civil Service Act.
The bill we have before us is interesting and the explanatory notes are also quite interesting. Some of the sections are given at great length while others are drafted in a very clever manner. The explanatory notes

also appear in length in respect of certain clauses of the bill while they are very brief in respect of other clauses. The draftsman of the bill is to be commended for the skill which he showed in his work.
Section 3 of the bill deals with the preference to persons on the list of pensioners; it relates to preferences to persons who served in the war. I might be in favour of certain clauses of this bill and I might quite well be in favour of this particular clause that gives a preference to Canadian soldiers who were domiciled in Canada prior to their enlistment. Section 3 of the bill reads as follows:
3. Subsection four of section twenty-nine of the said act is repealed, and the following is substituted therefor:-[DOT]
(4) In all examinations for entrance into the civil service the persons named on such special list who are found to possess the necessary qualifications shall be named, in the order of merit, on the list of successful candidates above all other candidates; and all other persons who have been on active service overseas on the military forces or who have served in the naval forces of His Majesty during the war, who had their domicile in Canada when they enlisted, and who, at the date of the coming into force of this act, have left such service with an honourable record or who have been honourably discharged, or when any persons who have served as aforesaid have died owing to such service, the widows of such persons, and who, in either case, obtain sufficient marks to pass such examinations, shall, irrespective of the marks they have obtained, be named in the order of merit on the list of successful candidates, next after any candidates who are on the special list mentioned in subsection two of this section and above all other candidates.
That section has some merit. It might be difficult to distinguish between those soldiers who were domiciled in Canada at the time of their enlistment and those who were not domiciled in Canada at that time, by virtue of the legal difficulties which might be involved in determining what constitutes domicile and when that domicile has been acquired.
I am opposed to section 5 of the bill, relating to promotions, and I am opposed to section 6 of the bill, relating to dismissals. I do not think we ought to encourage dismissals of civil servants by ministers, particularly when the Civil Service Act contains no provision for reinstatement of persons who have been dismissed. We may, by encouraging such dismissals, do even more injustices than have been done in the past. And I am heartily opposed to section 7 of the bill, which proposes that positions in the outside service shall be excluded from the operation of the act. The proposed subsection that is to be inserted in the new bill reads as follows:
63. The outside service shall be excluded from the operation of this act, and the
governor in council may make regulations for the control and direction, organization, classification and compensation, appointments to and general conditions of the outside service.
That means that in respect of the whole civil service outside Ottawa the Civil Service Act is scrapped, and that is a return to patronage in the whole of the outside service without any qualification whatsoever. To that I am absolutely opposed, and I am quite certain that the government does not favour any such action. I am quite certain that the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) is not in favour of any return to patronage in respect of the outside service. Why should we return to patronage? It is a reversion to a system from which we tried to escape when we began the effort to establish a proper civil service system in this country. Admittedly that system is imperfect. Admittedly we have not as yet reached the stage when we can say that it is a merit system. But surely the course we ought to follow in this matter is to remedy as much as possible the defects in our service and to reach our objective as soon as we can, rather than to destroy what has been accomplished and revert to a system which would be much worse than the imperfect system which we now have.
I do not think for a moment that control of patronage has any particular value, even to the member who controls the patronage. We as private members have a great many things to do; we have a tremendous volume of correspondence to attend to, and we are not qualified as other persons may be to make the most suitable selections for positions in the civil service. I think we should encourage improvements in the civil service rather than seek to destroy it, and we would be destroying it in respect of that whole portion outside Ottawa if we were to pass section 7 of this bill. The country does not desire any return to the patronage system; it would not improve the service of Canada. It would not help a single member to be re-elected. We sold in Canada from the coast region of British Columbia over one billion feet board measure; of this about 40 per cent was sold in our own province; we shipped 36 per cent to our neighbours on the prairies, for whom incidentally we have a very high regard, and we shipped 25 per cent to eastern Canada. Our next best customer was the United States, where we sold 540 million feet, or just a little over half of what we sold in the home market. We sold in foreign countries, other than the United States, 240 million feet, and we sold to empire countries 160 million feet.
I carry hon. members along two years further to 1931, and I am skipping the intervening year not in order to avoid anything, but simply to save time, because the trend of the figures is practically the same from year to year. In 1931 our best market was still Canada. We sold just over 520 million feet in Canada in that depression year as compared with a little over the billion feet in 1929. By this time eastern Canada had replaced the prairies as our second best home market. We sold the United States 270 million feet although the Hawley-Smoot tariff had come into effect and there was a duty of $1 per thousand feet against our lumber. We sold to foreign countries 200 million feet, and to the empire 160 million feet. The last figure was the same as in 1929 largely because of the activities of the lumbermen in British Columbia.
Then we come to 1932. In this year our best market was still in Canada, but sales had dropped from 520 million feet to 360 million feet. For the first time the British empire was our second best market, sales there coming up to 250 million feet. This increase was brought about by the fact that we received a preference of 10 per cent under the Canada-United Kingdom trade agreement. The foreign market had decreased to 115 million feet and the United States market had dropped to 70 million feet. One of the

reasons for this drop was the fact that on June 21, 1932, the United States put into effect an excise tax of $3 per thousand feet. The hon. member for Dauphin said last night that this excise tax was in retaliation for our tariffs, but that is not the case. That excise tax was an emergency measure. The building trade in the United States had slowed up and the Americans were unable to get rid of their lumber, so they effectively stopped the importation of Canadian lumber. Incidentally, that tax was only temporary; it was renewed in 1935, and I believe it will come up for consideration again in 1937. At that time we hope the United States will see fit to take it off entirely.
We come now to 1935. Our best market in that year was the British empire, our trade having gone up to 640 million feet, four times what it was in 1929. This increase occurred despite four years of depression. Our home trade was now in second place, the total being 560 million feet; this trade had improved with conditions. Our foreign trade had come up to 160 million feet and there had also been an improvement in the trade with the United States to 100 million feet.
Under the Canada-United States trade agreement both the excise tax and the duty are cut in half. Instead of $4 per thousand feet we shall have to pay only $2, and let me say here that that will be a great help to the producers in British Columbia. I give the government credit for giving us that much assistance. However, there is a quota of 250 million feet.

That applies only to
Douglas fir and hemlock.

I was just going to explain
that. This quota of 250 million feet applies only to Douglas fir and hemlock, although it must be remembered that in 1929 we sold the United States twice the amount of this quota. Quotas are something new to Canada. I believe this is the first time that one has ever been placed against us by the United States. I ask hon. members not to be misled during the next few months by the increases in lumber shipments to the United States, because at the present time lumber exporters are rushing lumber to that country in order to get their own lumber in before the quota is used up.
I should like the committee to compare that quota of 250 million feet with the sales to the empire totalling 640 million feet. This comparison will give the whole picture in a nutshell. It will show why the lumbermen of British Columbia are more concerned with the empire agreements than they are with

Canada-U. S. Trade Agreement
the Canada-United States agreement. The empire trade is far more important than the trade with the United States, because in empire trade there is great room for expansion while in the case of the United States we are met with the quota. Russia, Sweden and the Baltic countries sell to the United Kingdom four times as much lumber as we do; this shows the vast possibilities for expansion in that market. Also our empire trade is not subject to the dangers confronting our trade with the United States. The chief competitors of British Columbia in the American market are the lumbermen of Washington and Oregon, and they offer stiff competition. I should like to give some figures in explanation of this competition. In 1929 these two states shipped 550 million feet of lumber to the British empire in competition with British Columbia; this was nearly three times as much as the sales of British Columbia. Last year as a result of the empire trade agreements, Washington and Oregon shipped only 70 million feet to empire countries as compared with the 550 million feet shipped in 1929; this was just about one-ninth of what we shipped. Naturally this has irritated the lumbermen of the two states in question. These people have a strong lobby in Washington, and if the Roosevelt administration is defeated, I believe there will be little doubt that the lumbermen and other interests will make short work of this Canada-United States agreement.
My own opinion is that there is more scope for the development of trade within the empire than with the United States. The products of that group of nations which we term the British commonwealth are of great variety. This is not the case with Canada and the United States. As I have said already, the lumber of British Columbia must compete with the lumber of Washington and Oregon. As the hon. member for Yale (Mr. Stirling) told us the other evening, British Columbia fruit must meet American competition. The same thing applies to the fruit of Ontario and Nova Scotia. Wheat and other grains from our prairies and the manufactured products of Ontario and Quebec must compete with similar products of the nation to the south. The same applies to the cattle of the west and the fish of the maritime provinces. Both Canada and the United States produce practically the same commodities and there are definite limitations to the expansion of trade. This is not the case within the empire.
Finally, I believe it will always be more satisfactory for us to deal within the empire. Just as sentiment helps in business, so does
it help in trade between nations. There is a certain sentimental feeling between the different countries comprising the British empire. We know we are not so apt to be cut off on short notice by any of our sister nations, which might happen in the case of the United States, whose dealings with us are on a cold-blooded bargaining basis and always have been.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, from what the hon. member, who has just spoken, (Mr. Green) has said, it would seem that in his opinion we have been discussing the relative merits of the Canada-United States agreement and the Canada-United Kingdom agreement, and that it was a matter of choosing between one or the other. Surely my hon. friend kpows that there is nothing of the kind at stake. If it can have both agreements British Columbia will be better off than by having only one, and the fact that there are possibilities of one agreement not continuing indefinitely applies equally to the other. There may arise circumstances which will occasion alterations in either agreement, and for that very reason we ought to be glad to have two strings to our bow instead of one.

I thought I made it clear
that I gave the Prime Minister every credit for this preference in the lumber trade. I simply wish to point out, from a non-partisan standpoint, altogether regardless of party, that it is absolutely vital to us-and I say this in case some question may come up next year or the year after with respect to the empire agreements-that we must have these empire agreements. They are absolutely vital to our lumber trade and are far more important than the agreement with the United States.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council

I want to
make it perfectly clear to my hon. friend that so far as the Canada-United Kingdom agreement is concerned it is in no way prejudiced or affected by this agreement. The greatest care was taken to see that nothing in this agreement should affect the Canada-United Kingdom agreement either at the present time or at any future time. I might add, however, that if in negotiating the agreement the government had not been restricted because of certain provisions in the Canada-United Kingdom agreement greater concessions might have been obtained from the United States with respect to this agreement. It was felt, however, that the Canada-United Kingdom agreement was there and should stand as it was in all its details, and it has been left in that way.

Canada-U. S. Trade Agreement

Perhaps I might refer to
the statement of my hon. friend from Vancouver South (Mr. Green) with regard to the question of quotas. Ordinarily I believe a quota means that beyond a certain point there is an absolute embargo or prohibition of imports. That is not the case in respect of any of these items. With regard to Douglas fir and western hemlock, the quota, so-called, applies to the 250,000,000 feet upon which there is a duty of $2 instead of $4 as before; but if fortunately we do reach that amount of 250,000,000 feet there is no prohibition of further exports to the United States; only any amount above 250,000,000 feet will fall under the regular tariff of $4. There is considerable room for improvement in the export of these two woods. In 1934 we exported to the United States 25,000,000 feet as compared with 548,000,000 feet in 1930. I repeat, therefore, that there is a great deal of room for improvement in connection with these two woods. I might also make this comment without offence:	My
hon. friend said that if a Republican administration came into office in the United States they would soon abolish the agreement. Well, this agreement was made with the one intention which I think should govern all trade agreements with other countries, namely, that the benefit is mutual. But if he fears that the United States will nullify this agreement, this shows at least that my hon. friends must think there was something advantageous to Canada in making the agreement.

The minister says that
when we have reached 250,000,000 feet in our exports there is nothing to prevent us from exporting more; there will be no embargo. For all practical purposes, so far as the lumbermen are concerned, as the minister understands, there is an embargo because we cannot ship our lumber and pay $4 a thousand.
We shipped 25,000,000 feet.
When the minister gave the comparative figures for 1930 and 1935, was he referring to calendar or fiscal years?
Fiscal years.

So that the minister should not be too optimistic as to the recovery which may be anticipated from the agreement, I would call his attention to the fact that in 1930 our exports of Douglas fir and western hemlock, amounting to 548,000,000 feet, came under the old Fordney-McCumber tariff, under which they were free, whereas

the exports of 1935, reduced to 25,000,000 feet, came under the Hawley-Smoot tariff, which was $4 per thousand. Under this agreement the item is not back to free, where it was under the Fordney-McCumber tariff, but is $2 instead of S4.
It is a great deal better than it was.
Oh, half a loaf is better than no bread.

The minister has referred to our exports in 1930, and we have that tabulation statement here on page 30, but of course in the comparison between 1930 and 1935, wherein I notice most hon. members have charged the former administration with
responsibility for the falling off of exports, it must be remembered that the Hawley-Smoot tariff came into effect early in 1930, and I think a more reasonable comparison might be drawn from the figures of 1931. I find that while, by the minister's own figures, we exported 252,271 head immediately following the Hawley-Smoot tariff of 1931, which cannot be charged to any weakness of the administration on this side of the line, our total exports of cows, calves, and 700-pound beef cattle fell to 36,908 from 252,000. As soon as the Hawley-Smoot tariff went into effect in 1931, I find that of beef cattle weighing 700 pounds or more we exported only 1,976. Of cattle one year old, 700 pounds, we exported 1,976 head only in the year immediately following the Hawley-Smoot tariff, whereas in the year 1935 before the present agreement we exported 27,746. So the Hawley-Smoot tariff evidently had considerable effect, as had the enormous destruction that occurred in the United States, when they destroyed their hogs as well, and of course the price increased with the temporary demand in 1935. At the present time it is true we have had a slight increase.
I wish to say to the government that this item is of some help to the cattle breeders in Canada, especially at times of temporary demand in the United States. It is not any help to us in years when their cattle are lower priced than ours, and I might point out that it is of no significant advantage and there are very few cattle breeders in Canada who would want to sacrifice other very important Canadian interests for this slight advantage we get in cattle. It is not in any way comparable with what Canada received prior to the Fordney-McCumber tariff in 1922. In essence it means merely that we have secured a market in the United States for cattle at li cents a pound in some classifications and 2 cents a pound in others, and we are paying from li to 2 cents a pound duty to export to the United States under this agreement half as many cattle as we sold to the United States prior to 1922 free of duty. Where we sold around 497,000, 500,000 head prior to 1922 free of duty, we have now the exceptional privilege of a place in the United States market for practically half that amount, or approximately 257,000 head. So far as the effect on our cattle industry is concerned, the temporary advantage as regards live cattle is of some slight assistance, but I think those who represent cattle breeders and those who might be cattle breeders will agree with me that the price recently has not reflected any great advantage to Canadian producers.

I think this committee, and certainly the people throughout Canada who have cattle for sale, will remember very well when, in 1930, my hon. friend the member for Dufferin-Simcoe (Mr. Rowe) and the right hon. leader of the opposition (Mr. Bennett) were crossing this country, they were weeping bitter tears, bemoaning the sad fate of those hundred thousand dairy cattle that were condemned to be milked on the banks of the Albany instead of on the banks of the St. Lawrence-, in spite of the fact that the farmers of Quebec and Ontario particularly, and the farmers of the maritimes and Manitoba to some extent, had been selling those cattle at prices between $125 and $150. It was not very long after that until a 1,400 pound cow would not carry herself to market, until farmers and dealers had to dig up some of the money to pay the freight on a 1,400 pound cow from the shipping point to a point like Winnipeg.
They killed them in the United States.
They killed them in the United States and they killed them in Canada too, but after they killed them the beef was not worth as much as the freight.
They were not worth anything over there.
That is no reason why we should throw them away here. We are a more careful people, perhaps. Anyway we destroyed the trade in them.
You would not think we were a more capable people if you looked at this agreement.

I said "more
careful," and if you look at some of our actions in the past five years you would think we are neither capable nor careful. But we have amended that, and to-day our cattle are going to market to be traded for something that is of value. It is true that in the fiscal year 1935 there was a great shortage of feed in many of the American middle-west states. Naturally there was a demand for some cattle to go from Canada, and the price was certainly a good deal higher than it had been for some time before that. That was a particular sort of circumstance operating at -that time, and I am afraid the price will not be as good now. I well remember, however, when beef cattle were being shipped out in large quantities, in 1930, just at the end of the fiscal year, and when they were worth eight cents a pound to the farmer at the shipping point. At that time my hon. friends were bewailing the ruination of the cattle industry; that was one of their principal cries in western Canada, -and probably in the east as well. It was not long before the wailing was of another kind, however. I think -this is one of the most valuable items ever put into any agreement, because it gives a certain outlet for a large number of cattle at what will be a comparatively good price. Prices may not be as high as we would like them, but certainly they will be a great deal better than when this and other outlets were lacking. I think the government are to be commended for having secured this reduction, and I know the cattlemen of both western and eastern Canada appreciate it.

I do not want to delay the item too long, but in answer to the hon. member for Melfort may I say that while in 1930 we exported probably 100,000 head of cattle, under this agreement we are limited to 20,000 head, so the assistance the dairy industry will receive through the export of our dairy cattle will not be very extensive.

Canada-U. S. Trade Agreement
We now have a quota of 20,000 head of dairy cattle, and they must be carefully inspected before they can be exported. As a matter of fact it takes about six months to get a cow ready to go to the United States now; she has to have all sorts of certificates. The regulations are almost as strict as they are in connection with their immigration. A cow must be inspected for tuberculosis and twice for Bang's disease, in case she might react from the first test. So this quota of
20,000	head limits the advantage to the fortunate few who have highly accredited, carefully inspected stock, almost in the same category as registered cattle. Therefore I say that this will not be of any very great general advantage to the dairy farmers at large, who have been shipping cattle to the United States market for the last three or four years.

Undoubtedly it would be
desirable to have a larger quota than 20,000, but at the same time that is a very substantial figure. The figures for 1929, which is as far back as I can go, show that under the Fordney-McCumber tariff of that time we exported only a little over 21,000 head of dairy cattle.

This is
very good as far as it goes, but of course the quota limits it.

It is not limited; we can
always export more, but not under these terms.

The cattle

It is interesting to note that in 1930 we exported 85,226 head of these cattle and in 1931 we exported 27,188 head. I should like to know what effort the government made to have this agreement include cattle weighing from 175 to 700 pounds.

Every effort was made to

I would feel remiss in my

I was interested in one shipment and I know it brought a good deal more than it would have brought on the Winnipeg market on the same day.
